questions.question: For a positive real number a, what does the $p$-test say about the improper integral $\int_{a}^{\infty} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$?
options: It converges if and only if $p \gt 1.$
It converges if and only if $p \lt 1.$
It converges if and only if $p = 1.$
It always converges for every real p.

questions.question: For a positive real number a, what does the $p$-test say about the improper integral $\int_{0}^{a} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$?
options: It converges if and only if $p \gt 1.$
It converges if and only if $p \ge 1.$
It always diverges for every real p.
It converges if and only if $p \lt 1.$

questions.question: Which conclusion follows from the $p$-test for $\int_{1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x$?
options: It diverges, since $p = 2$ > 1.
It converges, since $p = 2$ < 1.
The infinity version of the test applies only when the lower bound is $0$.
It converges, since $p = 2$ > 1.

questions.question: Which conclusion follows from the $p$-test for $\int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x$?
options: It diverges, since $p = 1$ is not less than 1.
It converges, since $p = 1.$
It converges, since the interval is finite.
The near-zero case uses the same condition $p > 1$ as the infinity case.

questions.question: Why must behaviour near infinity and behaviour near zero be treated separately in the $p$-test?
options: Because the same endpoint condition is used after changing variables.
Because changing the endpoint changes the sign of $p$.
Because the convergence conditions are different: $p > 1$ at infinity and $p < 1$ near zero.
Because finite upper bounds remove all possible singular behaviour.

questions.question: What determines convergence for the improper integrals $\int_{a}^{\infty} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\int_{0}^{a} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$?
options: Only the numerical value of a.
Only the interval type and the value of p.
Only whether p is an integer.
Only whether the integrand is written using x or t.

questions.question: Use the $p$-test to classify ∫_3^∞ 1/$\sqrt{t}$ dt.
options: It converges, because $p = 1/2$ < 1.
It converges, because 3 is positive.
It diverges, because square roots are not allowed in the $p$-test.
It diverges, because $p = 1/2$ is not greater than 1.

questions.question: Use the $p$-test to classify ∫_0^2 1/$\sqrt{t}$ dt.
options: It diverges, because $p = 1/2$ < 1.
It converges, because $p = 1/2$ < 1.
It converges, because $p = 1/2$ > 1.
It diverges, because the upper bound is 2.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the boundary case $p = 1$ in the $p$-test?
options: It converges at infinity but diverges near zero.
It diverges both at infinity and near zero.
It diverges at infinity but converges near zero.
It converges both at infinity and near zero.

questions.question: A student says: “If $\int_{a}^{\infty} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges for a certain p, then $\int_{0}^{a} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$ also converges for the same p.” What is wrong with this claim?
options: Convergence at infinity would require the same inequality as convergence near zero.
The near-zero integral has no singularity whenever $a$ is positive.
The value of $a$ changes the exponent $p$.
The $p$-test gives opposite strict inequalities for the two endpoint behaviours.

questions.question: For which value of p does $\int_{1}^{\infty} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converge while $\int_{0}^{1} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges?
Which pair of conclusions is correct for $p = 1/2$?
options: $\int_{1}^{\infty} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges and $\int_{0}^{1} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges.
$\int_{1}^{\infty} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges and $\int_{0}^{1} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges.
$\int_{1}^{\infty} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges and $\int_{0}^{1} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges.
$\int_{1}^{\infty} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges and $\int_{0}^{1} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges.

questions.question: For $\int_a^{+\infty}t^{-p}\,dt$ with $a \gt 0$, what is the convergence condition?
options: $p \gt 1$
$p \lt 1$
$p \lt 0$

questions.question: For $\int_0^a t^{-p}\,dt$ with $a \gt 0$, what is the convergence condition?
options: $p \lt 1$
$p \gt 1$
$p \gt 0$ only

questions.question: What does the $p$-test classify?
options: Convergence of finite sums of real numbers
Convergence of power-type improper integrals
Continuity of polynomial functions everywhere
Proper subset relations between two sets

questions.question: Use the $p$-test to classify $\displaystyle\int_2^{\infty}\frac{1}{t^3}\,dt$.
options: It diverges because $p=3 \gt 1$
It converges because $p=3 \gt 1$
It converges because $p \lt 1$
It diverges because the lower bound is $2$

questions.question: Use the $p$-test to classify $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{1}{t^{1/3}}\,dt$.
options: It diverges because $p=\frac{1}{3}<1$.
It converges because $p=\frac{1}{3}<1$.
It uses the infinity condition $p>1$ even near zero.
It diverges because only integer exponents are allowed.

questions.question: Use the $p$-test to classify $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{1}{t^2}\,dt$.
options: It converges because $p=2 \gt 1$
It diverges because $p=2$ is not less than $1$
It converges because the interval is bounded
It diverges only when $p \lt 0$

questions.question: Why do $\int_a^{\infty}t^{-p}\,dt$ and $\int_0^a t^{-p}\,dt$ have opposite-looking conditions?
options: They test different problematic endpoints: infinity versus zero
They are actually the same improper integral
The exponent $p$ changes sign automatically
The value of $a$ determines the inequality direction

questions.question: For which real values of $q$ does $\displaystyle\int_1^{\infty}t^{-(q+2)}\,dt$ converge?
options: $q \gt 1$
